passages.happening: ‘Now Solomon son of David established himself securely over his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and highly exalted him’ (verse 1). He speaks to all Israel, its commanders, judges and family heads, and they go together to the high place at Gibeon, ‘because it was the location of God’s Tent of Meeting, which Moses the servant of the LORD had made in the wilderness’ (verse 3). The ark is already in Jerusalem, in the tent David pitched for it (verse 4), but the bronze altar made by Bezalel stands at Gibeon. ‘So Solomon and the assembly inquired of Him there’ (verse 5), and Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Second Chronicles begins where 1 Chronicles ended: David has died and Solomon reigns, usually dated about 970 to 930 BC. The first thing the Chronicler records is that Solomon sought God; the word inquired is darash, the book's mark of a faithful king. This chapter is the doorway into nine chapters on Solomon, and from chapter 2 the story turns almost entirely to the temple.

First Kings 1 to 3 tells more: the bloody securing of Solomon's throne, with the deaths of Adonijah, Joab and Shimei, his marriage to Pharaoh's daughter, and the note that people were still sacrificing at high places. The Chronicler compresses it all into one line, that Solomon established himself securely. His readers had Kings; he was drawing out what they needed.

A high place was an outdoor shrine, often on a hill. Later, high places became tied to idolatry and reforming kings tore them down, so the Chronicler explains why this one was right: the Tent of Meeting and the bronze altar of Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle, stood there. Gibeon lay about six miles north-west of Jerusalem, at the site called el-Jib, where excavators found a large rock-cut pool and jar handles inscribed with the town's name. For a time worship was divided between the altar at Gibeon and the ark in Jerusalem, until the temple brought them together.
passages.later: First Chronicles had said that the tabernacle of the LORD was ‘at the high place in Gibeon’ (1 Chronicles 21:29), and First Kings says that Solomon ‘went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for it was the great high place’ (1 Kings 3:4).
passages.asks: The first act of Solomon's reign was to gather the people and seek God. Ask what comes first when something new begins in your life. And ask whom you bring with you when you go to seek him.

passages.t: God offers, and Solomon asks for wisdom
passages.happening:
That night God appears to Solomon and says, “Ask, and I will give it to you!” (verse 7). Solomon remembers God's loving devotion to David and asks that God's promise to David be fulfilled (verses 8-9). Then: “Now grant me wisdom and knowledge, so that I may lead this people. For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?” (verse 10).

God answers that Solomon did not ask for riches, wealth, honor, the death of his enemies or long life, but for wisdom to govern God's people, ‘therefore wisdom and knowledge have been granted to you. And I will also give you riches and wealth and honor unlike anything given to the kings before you or after you’ (verse 12). Solomon returns to Jerusalem and reigns (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Ancient kings often sought a god's guidance at the start of a reign, sometimes through a dream at a sanctuary. The conversation turns on one verb, ask. God invites, Solomon asks for wisdom, and God names what he did not ask for before giving both.

Wisdom, chokhmah, covers skill in a craft, shrewd judgment and moral insight: seeing how things work and acting rightly. It is the governing word of Proverbs, much of which is linked with Solomon. Knowledge, madda, is a rare word, found mostly in late books such as Daniel and Ecclesiastes; joined with wisdom it means the discernment to understand people and situations well enough to govern them. Solomon begins by naming God's loving devotion, chesed, to David. His whole reign rests on it.

The request is not for Solomon's own sake but for the people's. He calls them God's people, not his.
passages.later: In First Kings Solomon asks, ‘Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil’ (1 Kings 3:9). Jesus said of the queen who came to hear Solomon, ‘she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here’ (Matthew 12:42). James wrote, ‘Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him’ (James 1:5).
passages.asks: Offered anything, Solomon asked for what he needed to serve others well. Ask what you would ask for if God made the same offer tonight. And ask whose good your prayers are mostly about.

passages.happening: ‘Solomon accumulated 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses’ (verse 14), stationed in the chariot cities and in Jerusalem. ‘The king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as abundant as sycamore in the foothills’ (verse 15). His horses come from Egypt and Kue, and his merchants sell chariots and horses on to the kings of the Hittites and of Aram (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
These lines stand near the end of Solomon's story in 1 Kings 10. The Chronicler sets them here, right after God's promise of riches, so the reader sees the promise kept at once, and a near copy returns at the end of his reign in chapter 9.

Horses and chariots were the most expensive military technology of the age. Kue is generally identified with Cilicia in south-eastern Anatolia, in modern Turkey, and the Hittite and Aramean kings were the small states of northern Syria. Verse 17 suggests that Solomon's merchants were middlemen in an international trade. Silver as common as stones is deliberate overstatement, the language of royal splendor.

The chapter reports all this without comment. See the hard question below.
passages.later: The law for Israel's kings said, ‘But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses’ (Deuteronomy 17:16), and ‘He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold’ (Deuteronomy 17:17).
passages.hard:
Didn't Solomon's horses from Egypt and his heaps of silver and gold break the law for Israel's kings?

The law warned that a king must not gather many horses or send to Egypt for them, and must not pile up silver and gold. These verses describe Solomon doing exactly that. Readers take it in different ways.

Some see the Chronicler, like the writer of Kings, quietly showing the seeds of Solomon's later troubles even while he celebrates the wealth; an attentive Israelite reader would have heard the echo of Deuteronomy. Others note that the verses come straight after God's promise of riches and read them simply as the promise kept, with the Chronicler choosing not to dwell on failures his readers already knew from 1 Kings 11. A minority of scholars suggest that Egypt in verses 16 and 17 may mean a region near Kue in Anatolia with a similar name.

On any reading the Chronicler does not deny Solomon's faults. He leaves them for Kings to tell, and leaves the shadow in plain view for those who know the rest of the story.
passages.asks: God gave Solomon riches, and the same riches would later test him. Ask which of God's good gifts to you could become a danger if you held it too tightly. And ask what you are gathering that God never asked you to gather.
